title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR): DeepSeek-R1 and Tülu 3

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied RLVR material contains only bibliographic entries and fragments, with no substantive authorial claims, findings or recommendations. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine whether the source accepts, extends or rejects the cluster’s proposition about benchmark quality, governance and workplace meaning.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied material is only bibliographic context. Although it cites work on automatic-evaluator bias, benchmark robustness, self-correction and reward-model overoptimization, it does not provide the source’s own methods, findings or endorsement of the cluster’s proposition that credible evaluation must test professional task execution and separately validate judging and self-correction.

st.t: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s methodological distinction by evaluating standard benchmark performance separately from open-ended generation judged through pairwise LLM comparisons. It also illustrates protocol sensitivity through a stated length-bias control and benchmark-specific prompt changes, but provides no results establishing that these measures eliminate bias or quantify prompt effects.
qs: In addition to standard benchmarks, we also evaluate our models on open-ended generation tasks using LLMs as judges.
Here, we only feed the final summary to evaluation to avoid the length bias.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s jagged-capability premise by reporting strong gains on some benchmarks alongside weaker general capabilities, mixed software-engineering results and prompt sensitivity. It does not directly address legal-work redesign, human verification or operating models, so its support is limited to the underlying technical rationale for selective, task-specific deployment.
qs: • General Capability: Currently, the capabilities of DeepSeek-R1 fall short of DeepSeek-V3 in tasks such as function calling, multi-turn, complex role-playing, and JSON output.
• Prompting Engineering: When evaluating DeepSeek-R1, we observe that it is sensitive to prompts.

kp.k: Reinforcement learning improves reasoning without preliminary supervised fine-tuning
kp.d: DeepSeek-AI reports applying reinforcement learning directly to the pretrained DeepSeek-V3-Base model to produce DeepSeek-R1-Zero. Its AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 71.0%; majority voting reached 86.7%. The absence of supervised fine-tuning concerns the post-training approach, not an absence of pretraining. These are reasoning-model findings, not evidence about legal work.
qs: Specifically, we use DeepSeek-V3-Base as the base model and employ GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) as the RL framework to improve model performance in reasoning.
For instance, the pass@1 score on AIME 2024 increases from 15.6% to 71.0%, and with majority voting, the score further improves to 86.7%, matching the performance of OpenAI-o1-0912.

kp.k: Rule-based rewards exploit tasks with checkable answers
kp.d: R1-Zero uses accuracy and formatting rewards: deterministic mathematical answers permit rule-based correctness checks, while coding tasks provide feedback from predefined tests. The authors avoid neural outcome and process reward models in this stage because of reward hacking, retraining costs and pipeline complexity. This mechanism concerns automated training feedback, rather than human checking of professional work.
qs: For example, in the case of math problems with deterministic results, the model is required to provide the final answer in a specified format (e.g., within a box), enabling reliable rule-based verification of correctness.
Similarly, for LeetCode problems, a compiler can be used to generate feedback based on predefined test cases.

We do not apply the outcome or process neural reward model in developing DeepSeek-R1-Zero, because we find that the neural reward model may suffer from reward hacking in the large-scale reinforcement learning process, and retraining the reward model needs additional training resources and it complicates the whole training pipeline.

kp.k: GRPO reduces training costs by eliminating a critic model
kp.d: The authors adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization to save reinforcement-learning training costs. Instead of maintaining a critic typically as large as the policy model, GRPO estimates a baseline from scores for a group of sampled outputs. The document describes this cost-saving mechanism without quantifying monetary savings.
qs: In order to save the training costs of RL, we adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024), which foregoes the critic model that is typically the same size as the policy model, and estimates the baseline from group scores instead.

kp.k: Longer reasoning and reflection emerge during reinforcement learning
kp.d: The authors report increasing response lengths during R1-Zero training and describe spontaneous reflection and exploration of alternative solutions. Their illustrated “aha moment” is an observation of generated behavior in an intermediate checkpoint, while claims about future autonomous and adaptive models are prospective interpretations.
qs: DeepSeek-R1-Zero naturally learns to solve reasoning tasks with more thinking time.
Behaviors such as reflection—where the model revisits and reevaluates its previous steps—and the exploration of alternative approaches to problem-solving arise spontaneously.
During this phase, DeepSeek-R1-Zero learns to allocate more thinking time to a problem by reevaluating its initial approach.

kp.k: Cold-start supervision addresses readability and language mixing
kp.d: R1-Zero's poor readability and mixed-language output motivate R1's four-stage pipeline: cold-start supervised fine-tuning, reasoning-oriented RL, rejection sampling and further supervised fine-tuning, then RL across scenarios. Thousands of cold-start examples incorporate readable model outputs and human refinement. A language-consistency reward improves readability but, according to ablation experiments, slightly degrades performance.
qs: The pipeline consists of four stages, outlined as follows.
In this work, we collect thousands of cold-start data to fine-tune the DeepSeek-V3-Base as the starting point for RL.
Although ablation experiments show that such alignment results in a slight degradation in the model’s performance, this reward aligns with human preferences, making it more readable.

kp.k: General-purpose alignment combines supervised data and mixed rewards
kp.d: Following reasoning RL, the authors collect about 600k reasoning samples and approximately 200k non-reasoning samples, then fine-tune DeepSeek-V3-Base for two epochs. Some expanded reasoning data receive judgments from DeepSeek-V3 rather than rule-based checks alone. Final RL combines rule-based rewards for reasoning with preference reward models for general tasks; helpfulness is assessed on the final summary, harmlessness on the entire response.
qs: For each prompt, we sample multiple responses and retain only the correct ones.
In total, we collect about 600k reasoning related training samples.
We fine-tune DeepSeek-V3-Base for two epochs using the above curated dataset of about 800k samples.
For general data, we resort to reward models to capture human preferences in complex and nuanced scenarios.

kp.k: Benchmark competitiveness varies across reasoning and engineering tasks
kp.d: The authors report R1 scoring 79.8% pass@1 on AIME 2024 and 97.3% on MATH-500, versus 79.2% and 96.4% for OpenAI-o1-1217. Table 4 reports 71.5% on GPQA Diamond versus o1's 75.7%, and 49.2% resolved on SWE-bench Verified versus 48.9%. R1 trails o1 on Aider-Polyglot, 53.3% versus 61.7%. Thus the paper's comparable-performance claim is task-dependent rather than universal superiority.
qs: DeepSeek-R1 achieves a score of 79.8% Pass@1 on AIME 2024, slightly surpassing OpenAI-o1-1217.
On MATH-500, it attains an impressive score of 97.3%, performing on par with OpenAI-o1-1217 and significantly outperforming other models.
On engineering-oriented coding tasks, OpenAI-o1-1217 outperforms DeepSeek-R1 on Aider but achieves comparable performance on SWE Verified.

kp.k: Benchmark results depend on sampling and evaluation protocols
kp.d: Evaluation caps generation at 32,768 tokens and estimates pass@1 from multiple sampled responses using temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, typically with 4–64 responses per question. AIME consensus results use 64 samples and are distinct from pass@1. LiveCodeBench covers August 2024–January 2025; Codeforces uses 10 Div.2 contests and expert-crafted tests. OpenAI-o1-1217 comparisons use official reports because of API-access difficulties, rather than the authors directly evaluating that model.
qs: We set the maximum generation length to 32,768 tokens for the models.
For AIME 2024, we also report consensus (majority vote) results (Wang et al., 2022) using 64 samples, denoted as cons@64.
The Codeforces dataset is evaluated using problems from 10 Div.2 contests along with expert-crafted test cases, after which the expected ratings and percentages of competitors are calculated.

kp.k: Distillation transfers reasoning capabilities to smaller models
kp.d: The authors fine-tune Qwen and Llama models using the curated 800k samples, releasing six distilled checkpoints from 1.5B to 70B parameters. Reported distilled-model results use supervised fine-tuning without RL. In their 32B comparison, direct RL for over 10K steps achieves 47.0% AIME pass@1, while distillation achieves 72.6%. They interpret this as evidence favoring distillation in the tested setting; their suggestion that pushing capability frontiers may require larger base models and RL remains conditional.
qs: For distilled models, we apply only SFT and do not include an RL stage, even though incorporating RL could substantially boost model performance.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B achieves 55.5% on AIME 2024, surpassing QwQ-32B-Preview.

Second, while distillation strategies are both economical and effective, advancing beyond the boundaries of intelligence may still require more powerful base models and larger- scale reinforcement learning.

kp.k: Process rewards and tree search encounter scaling limitations
kp.d: The authors describe unsuccessful attempts with process reward models and Monte Carlo Tree Search. Process rewards face difficulties defining and judging intermediate steps, scaling annotation and avoiding reward hacking. Tree search faces an exponentially large token-generation space, local optima under expansion limits and difficult value-model training. These are limitations of their experiments, not a claim that either approach cannot work.
qs: We share our failure experiences here to provide insights, but this does not imply that these approaches are incapable of developing effective reasoning models.
First, it is challenging to explicitly define a fine-grain step in general reasoning.

In conclusion, while MCTS can improve performance during inference when paired with a pre-trained value model, iteratively boosting model performance through self-search remains a significant challenge.

kp.k: Deployment limitations qualify broad reasoning gains
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that R1 trails DeepSeek-V3 in function calling, multi-turn interaction, complex role-playing and JSON output. Optimization for Chinese and English leaves other-language mixing problems. They recommend zero-shot instructions specifying the problem and output format because few-shot prompting degrades performance. Software-engineering RL remains constrained by long evaluation times; rejection sampling and asynchronous evaluation are proposed future improvements, not demonstrated remedies.
qs: Currently, the capabilities of DeepSeek-R1 fall short of DeepSeek-V3 in tasks such as function calling, multi-turn, complex role-playing, and JSON output.
Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
Therefore, we recommend users directly describe the problem and specify the output format using a zero-shot setting for optimal results.
Future versions will address this by implementing rejection sampling on software engineering data or incorporating asynchronous evaluations during the RL process to improve efficiency.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: DeepSeek-AI claims that reinforcement learning can improve model reasoning without preliminary supervised fine-tuning, that its multi-stage R1 model achieves reasoning performance comparable to OpenAI o1, and that distillation transfers strong reasoning performance to smaller models.
pts.d: These are cross-domain claims about AI model development, not legal services. The supplied substantive text is DeepSeek-R1 arXiv:2501.12948v1; although the document heading mentions Tülu 3 and a Nature publication, no substantive Tülu 3 text or later Nature version is supplied. DeepSeek-AI reports that R1-Zero develops reflection, longer reasoning outputs and alternative problem-solving approaches through RL. R1 adds cold-start examples and multiple supervised and reinforcement-learning stages to improve performance and readability. The authors also claim broader benefits for document analysis, search, writing and question answering. They describe distillation as an economical and effective way to improve smaller models, while suggesting that advancing frontier capabilities may require stronger base models and larger-scale RL. Future software-engineering improvements are predictions rather than reported results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of developer-reported benchmark results, training observations and a comparison of distillation with direct RL on a 32B model.
pts.d: DeepSeek-AI reports R1-Zero's AIME 2024 pass@1 increasing from 15.6% to 71.0%, with 86.7% under 64-sample majority voting; these are distinct metrics. Table 4 reports R1 at 79.8% AIME pass@1 versus o1-1217's 79.2%, 97.3% MATH-500 versus 96.4%, and 49.2% SWE-bench Verified resolved versus 48.9%. Results are not uniformly superior: R1 scores 71.5% on GPQA Diamond versus o1-1217's 75.7%, and 53.3% on Aider-Polyglot versus 61.7%. R1's FRAMES accuracy is 82.5%, compared with V3's 73.3%. Open-ended writing and question-answering claims draw on GPT-4-Turbo-1106 judgments in AlpacaEval 2.0 and ArenaHard, not human workplace outcome studies. The o1-1217 comparison uses official reports because of API-access difficulties. Table 6 compares a Qwen-32B model trained for over 10,000 RL steps with the distilled 32B model: AIME pass@1 is 47.0% versus 72.6%, respectively. The 'aha moment' is illustrated by a generated response and supported by observations of increasing response length; it is not evidence of human-like subjective experience. No legal-service outcomes, labour-market effects or quantified deployment savings are measured.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern the January 2025 model release under specified training and evaluation conditions; proposed improvements have no firm delivery date.
pts.d: The supplied paper is dated 22 January 2025, and its LiveCodeBench evaluation covers August 2024–January 2025. R1-Zero's absence of preliminary SFT does not mean absence of a pretrained base model: it starts from DeepSeek-V3-Base. Its rule-based rewards check deterministic mathematical answers, code test results and output formatting. These automated training checks and the model's self-checking should not be equated with human verification of professional work. R1 is not exclusively trained with rule-based rewards: its broader pipeline also uses supervised examples and learned reward models for general scenarios. Evaluations allow up to 32,768 generated tokens, use temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, and estimate pass@1 from multiple sampled responses. Distilled-model results principally reflect SFT on approximately 800,000 curated examples, without an RL stage. The authors acknowledge weaker function calling, multi-turn interaction and JSON output than V3, language mixing beyond Chinese and English, and sensitivity to prompting. Software-engineering RL is constrained by long evaluation times. Claims about future engineering gains, further RL on distilled models and more autonomous models are forward-looking and undated.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries are AI researchers, model developers and users of reasoning and general-purpose AI tools; legal-sector effects are not specified.
pts.d: DeepSeek-AI presents the released R1, R1-Zero and six distilled Qwen/Llama models as resources for researchers and developers seeking stronger reasoning capabilities and smaller models. It suggests that software developers could benefit from engineering performance, and that document-analysis, search and data-analysis applications could benefit from improved long-context reasoning. General users are intended to benefit from clearer output and alignment with preferences, while users outside Chinese and English face language-mixing limitations. The paper makes no concrete claim about lawyers, law firms, ALSPs, legal clients, professional staffing, legal pricing or access to justice.
